html:
The arrival in 166 of men claiming to be envoys from the king of Daqin, the Chinese name for the Roman Empire, at the court of the Han emperor. The king is named Andun, which most scholars read as Marcus Aurelius Antoninus.

The Book of the Later Han records that they came by sea through Rinan, a Chinese frontier province in what is now central Vietnam. They brought ivory, rhinoceros horn and tortoiseshell. The Chinese noted that these were goods of Southeast Asia, not Roman treasures, so the visitors were probably merchants who called themselves envoys.

It is the first recorded direct contact between the two empires. Rome and China knew of each other mostly through middlemen: silk crossed Asia along the Silk Road and spices came by the Indian Ocean. A Chinese envoy, Gan Ying, had tried to reach Rome in 97 but turned back at the Persian Gulf.
